questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the sequence in which a party fills its leadership offices.
questions.stem: Your survey team's report on a regional party notes that the membership elects a president, who then appoints a secretary and a treasurer from among the elected executive. Which sequence of selection is at work?

options.text: Members elect a leader first, and that leader then appoints the remaining executive officers.
A single stage in which the whole membership elects every officer in the same meeting.
options.misconception: misses that the executive posts are appointed, not elected

options.text: A reversed order in which a treasurer appoints the president and the president then ratifies it.
options.misconception: invents an appointment chain the scenario never describes

options.text: A random selection in which party members draw names from a hat to fill the executive posts.
options.misconception: assumes randomness where a stated election takes place

questions.explanation: The report separates choosing the leader from filling the other offices, so selection runs in two stages. Because the leader appoints colleagues from the elected executive, the second stage follows the first.
questions.hint: Ask who chooses whom, and in what order.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the features of a cartel system in a local resource arrangement.

stimulus.body: Survey station record: 'The valley's two established associations have used the same hall for forty years under an unwritten arrangement. The rota alternates the chair between them, the two clerks share one filing cabinet, and new associations are told by both that the hall is fully subscribed. Neither association has ever applied jointly for the additional space, although the extension was built in 1996.'

questions.stem: Given the field note, which features of a cartel system are evident in this arrangement?

options.text: The two associations compete for membership, because the shared hall is contested each season.
options.misconception: assumes competition where a rotation is described

options.text: Insiders share scarce resources, divide the offices, and deter newcomers without any formal rule.
The associations have merged, because they share a filing cabinet and a building.
options.misconception: confuses resource sharing with a formal merger

options.text: The hall's management is democratic, because the extension of the building was voted on.
options.misconception: assumes a building decision implies democratic management

questions.explanation: The rota, the shared cabinet and the discouragement of newcomers are the features of a cartel. Nothing formal was ever agreed, and sharing a building is not a merger.
questions.hint: Look for the three habits the note records.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why two competing parties converge on the positions of the median voter.
questions.stem: Along one transect of your survey area, the two main parties have identical manifestos on grazing quotas and road funding, though they differ on whether to fund a new research station. What is the likely mechanism behind this?

options.text: A legal ban on policy differences, because the parties must publish matching programmes.
options.misconception: assumes a legal requirement for matching policies

options.text: A shared membership list, because the parties have merged their voter registers.
options.misconception: assumes a shared register explains identical policies

options.text: Convergence towards the median voter, who wants few policy differences on spending.
A single-issue revolt, because voters abandoned both programmes for a third cause.
options.misconception: mistakes similarity between parties for a new third cause

questions.explanation: When two parties seek the same median voter they converge on the policies that voter favours and differ only where the median is indifferent. The shared position on spending with disagreement on the new station is exactly that pattern.
questions.hint: Ask which voter both parties are courting.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a closed primary mechanism selects a party candidate.
questions.stem: In the county you survey, a party chooses its candidate for the county council in a contest open only to members who joined before a fixed date. Explain how this mechanism works and what it produces.

answer.exemplar: The closed primary narrows the electorate to the existing membership, defined by a joining date rather than by any test of support. Candidates are nominated by a specified number of members and then ranked by a ballot sent to that membership. Two things follow. The result reflects the preferences of people already committed to the party, which is often a small and well-organised group, and the process gives the party a candidate it can present with some confidence because the choice has been ratified internally. The mechanism therefore trades representativeness of the selection for internal coherence and the avoidance of a contest that a hostile outside group might capture.

questions.explanation: A closed primary defines the electorate by membership as at a fixed date, so only committed members choose. It produces a candidate the party can present confidently, at the cost of a narrow selection.
questions.hint: Ask who is allowed on the ballot's electorate.

options.misconception: assumes a single seat implies an absolute majority

options.text: It guarantees that the election was contested, because nomination papers were submitted.
options.misconception: infers contestation from the existence of papers

options.text: It guarantees that the declared candidate will hold the seat for the full term.
options.misconception: confuses election with the duration of the term

options.text: It guarantees that exactly one person will take the seat, whoever the votes support.

questions.explanation: A division returning one member guarantees a single occupant of the seat, whatever the votes decide. The extract shows an unopposed return, which is why no count was needed, and says nothing about majorities.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the level at which a proportional allocation operates.
questions.stem: A proportional list in your region allocates seats to parties in proportion to votes, but within each district a single member is chosen. What does the proportional element guarantee?

options.text: That the chamber as a whole reflects the distribution of votes across parties, not one district's result.
That each individual member represents the majority view of their own district.
options.misconception: assumes proportional lists give every seat a local majority

options.text: That every party that wins votes in a district wins a seat in that district.
options.misconception: assumes proportionality guarantees local representation

options.text: That no party can ever gain or lose seats when boundaries are redrawn.
options.misconception: claims boundary changes cannot alter party totals

questions.explanation: Proportionality is a property of the chamber as a whole, tying seats to the overall distribution of votes. It says nothing about any single district, because list allocation works across the whole vote.
questions.hint: Ask what the guarantee covers.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess a claim that confidence-and-supply agreements strengthen government stability.
questions.stem: A review argues that a confidence-and-supply agreement between two parties makes a minority government more stable than a single-party majority would be, because the minority depends on support it must keep earning. Evaluate that argument for a briefing note.

answer.exemplar: The argument identifies a real virtue of minority government, because a government that needs weekly support has incentives to keep its majority partner satisfied, and that constraint can produce more disciplined policy than a comfortable majority. But it misidentifies what is being guaranteed. The agreement is a bargain between the parties, and its stability depends on the continued agreement of both partners, not on any institutional protection for the minority. That makes the arrangement's durability contingent on the personalities and politics of two sets of negotiators. A single-party majority also faces a check, in the electorate at the next election, and it is not evident that a fixed partisan pact is always the better answer. The real question is whether the minority's need for support produces better scrutiny of policy or merely a narrowing of the government's freedom to act.

questions.explanation: The argument rightly notes that minority governments must keep earning support, but confuses a bargain with a guarantee. Stability then depends on two sets of negotiators rather than on the structure of the chamber.
questions.hint: Ask what makes the agreement last.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify a caretaker government from how it conducts business.
questions.stem: After a general election in the county you are surveying, no party has been able to form a government, and an existing administration continues to handle current business without entering new policies. What is this arrangement?

options.text: A coalition government, because two or more parties are sharing executive power.
options.misconception: assumes shared power where none is shared

options.text: A caretaker government, because it manages existing business while a new ministry is formed.
A minority government, because the administration lacks a legislative majority.
options.misconception: confuses lacking a majority with lacking a settled mandate

options.text: An emergency government, because ordinary decision-making has been suspended.
options.misconception: presumes emergency powers where routine duties continue

questions.explanation: A caretaker administration conducts current business without new policy decisions while a successor is settled. Power is not shared, so it is not a coalition, and lacking a majority is true of many formed governments.
questions.hint: Ask whether new policy is being made.

questions.stem: According to the association record, which order of selection applies?

options.misconception: reverses the sequence the record sets out

options.text: The president appoints two field officers who then elect a secretary from among themselves.
options.misconception: misplaces the secretary's place in the chain

options.text: Delegates elect the president, the president appoints a secretary, and the secretary nominates field officers.
Every officer is elected at the annual meeting, with the appointment powers serving only as fallbacks.
options.misconception: treats stated appointment powers as unused fallbacks

questions.explanation: The record sets a chain: delegates elect the president, who appoints a secretary, who nominates field officers. Each step follows the last, and the annual meeting can change the sequence but has not done so.
questions.hint: Trace the sequence step by step.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a cartel arrangement reproduces itself without a formal agreement.
questions.stem: In the settlement where you are working, two long-established families have run the grazing commons in rotation for three generations, share a hired shepherd, and are each other's rivals in the parish council. Explain what makes this arrangement self-reproducing.

answer.exemplar: The arrangement reproduces itself because each feature solves a problem for both families. The rotation prevents a costly fight over the commons, and the shared shepherd keeps the cost of labour below what either family would bear alone. Membership is closed and hereditary in practice, because the skills of managing the commons are passed to the young of the same two families and there is no route in for anyone else. The rivalry in the parish council is not disruptive either, since both families know that the commons arrangement gives them each a guaranteed share, and they are careful never to push that advantage to the point of open conflict. The system thus holds together through mutual gain and mutual veto, and it needs no written rule to do so.

questions.explanation: Each element removes a reason to defect: rotation avoids open conflict and shared costs keep the bargain efficient. Closure of membership and rivalry elsewhere follow from that bargain rather than contradicting it.
questions.hint: Ask why neither side would want to break it.

options.misconception: reads a policy gap as a separate party identity

options.text: The parties differ because the levy has already been settled and no longer matters to anyone.
options.misconception: assumes a settled issue stops mattering to voters

options.text: The parties differ on fishery rules because the larger party forced the smaller to differentiate.
options.misconception: invents party pressure the survey does not show

options.text: The parties converge where the median voter has a strong interest, and diverge where it does not.

questions.explanation: Convergence is strongest where the median voter's preferences are intense, since both parties must please that voter. Where the median is indifferent, the parties can differ freely without much electoral cost.
questions.hint: Ask where the median voter's interest lies.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what proportional allocation guarantees and what it leaves unresolved.
questions.stem: Your briefing note must explain to a new district what a proportional list system guarantees about the relationship between votes and seats, and what it leaves unresolved.

answer.exemplar: A proportional list system converts votes into seats across the whole electorate at once, so the share of seats a party holds tracks the share of votes it won, within the precision the divisor allows. That is the guarantee: the composition of the chamber as a whole reflects the distribution of votes among parties, and a party that doubles its vote will not end up with fewer seats. What it does not guarantee is anything about individual districts, because the list is drawn nationally and a party may win a district in votes and still not field a candidate there. Nor does it eliminate the distortions of a first-past-the-post count where a separate set of seats is filled that way. Proportionality is a statement about the chamber, not about any place within it.

questions.explanation: The guarantee is chamber-level: seats track votes across the whole electorate. Individual districts remain unresolved, because lists are drawn nationally and no local candidate is assured.
questions.hint: Ask whether the claim is about seats or about places.

options.misconception: assumes a supply agreement creates a working majority

options.text: The government has been forced to resign, because the assembly withheld its confidence.
options.misconception: reads a negotiated support as a loss of confidence

options.text: The government keeps office while the opposition supplies support in return for a policy concession.
A coalition has been formed, because two parties now share the executive outright.
options.misconception: confuses supply of votes with sharing of executive posts

questions.explanation: The minute records conditional support for specified measures in return for a named policy, with the government still in office. That is confidence and supply, not a coalition, since the executive has not been shared.
questions.hint: Check who holds the executive afterwards.

options.misconception: gives the caretaker a mandate the description denies it

options.text: A minority government, because it lacks the votes to command the assembly's confidence.
options.misconception: confuses a temporary administration with a formed minority

options.misconception: assumes sharing of decisions in a caretaker period

options.text: A caretaker government, because it manages existing business without taking new policy decisions.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Design a district arrangement that secures representation without losing accountability.
questions.stem: Your survey has revealed that voters in scattered settlements feel remote from a single large constituency. Propose an arrangement that keeps each district to a single member while improving the connection between the member and the area.

answer.exemplar: Keep the single-member rule and change the shape of the seat rather than the number of members. A smaller constituency, with the boundaries drawn around a coherent settlement rather than a countywide sweep, lets a single member plausibly know every parish in the seat. Second, set the candidacy rule so that a candidate must have a connection to the area, for example a residence or a business in the constituency, which makes the member answerable to a recognisable community. Third, publish a regular constituency schedule and a written record of the member's casework, so that a voter can see what the member has actually done for their settlement. None of this changes the guarantee that one place has one member, and each measure attacks the remoteness that made the guarantee feel thin in the first place.

questions.explanation: The single-member rule can be kept while its costs are reduced through smaller seats and a residency condition. A published casework record adds to that, and no measure adds a second member to the delegation.
questions.hint: Change the shape, not the number of seats.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the remit and limits of a caretaker government.
questions.stem: In the district you survey, a caretaker administration has been in office for six weeks while a new coalition is negotiated. Explain what such an administration may and may not do, and why the limit exists.

answer.exemplar: A caretaker administration exists to keep the state running without making new commitments, because a government that is only in office provisionally should not bind its successors to irreversible decisions. Routine matters continue: existing contracts are honoured, existing law is administered, and ministers answer questions in the assembly. Discretionary and forward-looking decisions are restricted, such as opening new programmes, signing long-term commitments or announcing major spending, since each of these would prejudge the choices the incoming government must make. The limit exists for two reasons at once. It protects the incoming government from inheriting policies it did not choose, and it protects the caretaker from being judged for decisions it had no mandate to take. Where a caretaker is given wider powers, as during an emergency or a simple administrative transition, the reasons for the restriction weaken and the justification for each act must be recorded.

questions.explanation: A caretaker keeps the machinery running but avoids decisions that bind a successor to new policy. The restriction protects the incoming government from inherited policy and the caretaker from unmandated acts.
questions.hint: Ask what a provisional government should promise.

questions.learningObjective: Read an order of selection from a written constitution.

stimulus.body: Constitution of the valley association, section 4: 'The committee shall be elected by the general meeting of members. The committee shall in turn elect the association's chair from among its own number, and the chair shall appoint the association's two trustees. Any alteration to this order requires a two-thirds vote of the general meeting.'

questions.stem: Which order of selection does section 4 establish?

options.text: Appointment of trustees first, then election of the committee to supervise them.
options.misconception: inverts the order the constitution sets out

options.text: Election of the chair by members, with the committee appointed afterwards by the chair.
options.misconception: treats the committee's election as an appointment

options.text: Election of the committee by members, which then elects the chair, who appoints the trustees.
Election of the whole committee and chair together at the general meeting, with trustees nominated.
options.misconception: assumes a single meeting fills every office

questions.explanation: Section 4 runs one way: members elect the committee, which elects the chair, who appoints the trustees. The two-thirds clause allows the order to be changed, but does not change the current sequence.
questions.hint: Read the sequence of verbs.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the combination of features that constitutes a cartel.
questions.stem: An established association in your survey area controls the only boat, employs most of the local crew, and has never allowed a rival onto the water. Which features does this combine?

options.text: A legal monopoly, because the association holds a statutory exclusive licence.
options.misconception: assumes a statutory licence where none is described

options.text: A scale advantage, because the association's boat is larger than any other.
options.misconception: focuses on boat size rather than exclusion

options.text: A democratic arrangement, since the crew are elected to serve the association.
options.misconception: reads an elected crew as democratic control of the association

options.text: Control of the key asset, of the labour, and of access for any competitor.

questions.explanation: The cartel features here are ownership of the indispensable asset, employment of the labour pool and exclusion of competitors from the resource. None of them requires a statute, a size advantage or internal elections, which are not described.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how convergence towards the median voter shapes party competition.
questions.stem: Using the preferences recorded in your survey, explain how the pursuit of the median voter shapes the competition between the two main parties, and note one limit of that explanation.

answer.exemplar: The two parties compete for the voter at the middle of the preference distribution, and because both need that vote to win, they are pulled towards the positions that voter holds most strongly and away from those the voter treats lightly. The road levy in the survey is an example: it is costly, widely noticed, and closely watched, so the party that proposes a different formula risks losing the median voter, and both proposals therefore sit close together. On waste collection, where most respondents place the issue low in their list of priorities, the parties can differ without much cost. The limitation of the explanation is that it predicts convergence on the median issue but not the exact policy, and it underplays the role of party identity, money and organisation in sustaining a distinct position where the median voter does not care.

questions.explanation: Both parties need the median voter's support, so they converge where that voter is sensitive and differ where indifferent. The account predicts the direction of convergence, not the exact policy that results.
questions.hint: Ask which voter decides the contest.

questions.learningObjective: Assess the effect of a closed primary on the character of the candidate chosen.
questions.stem: In the closed contest held in the town you survey, only members of five years' standing could vote, and the candidate list was drawn by a nominating committee. What does the arrangement deliver?

options.text: A candidate chosen by a narrow, committed group, with limited scope for outside influence.
A candidate chosen by the widest possible range of the party's supporters.
options.misconception: reads a restricted electorate as a wide one

options.text: A candidate selected by an open ballot in the constituency as a whole.
options.misconception: confuses a party primary with a public election

options.text: A candidate appointed by the party's executive without any ballot at all.
options.misconception: ignores the ballot that the arrangement still includes

questions.explanation: A five-year standing rule plus a committee-drawn list confines both the voters and the options to a narrow body of committed members. That delivers internal consolidation, and it removes almost any opportunity for influence from outside the established group.
questions.hint: Look at who votes and who lists.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the single-member guarantee to a reported count.

stimulus.body: Observation from the counting centre: 'Three candidates were returned for the river ward. questions.stem: What does the observation establish about the river ward's arrangement?

options.text: The seat was correctly filled, because the first candidate obtained more than half of all votes cast.
options.misconception: assumes the leader of a three-way race holds a majority

options.text: One member will take the seat, chosen by the largest vote, with no absolute majority needed.
The count must be repeated, because the turnout was below half of the registered electors.
options.misconception: treats a low turnout as a trigger for a recount

options.text: The three candidates will share the ward between them, since the ward covers a wide area.
options.misconception: assumes a multi-member allocation the ward does not have

questions.explanation: The ward returns one member and the rule is the greatest number of votes, so one occupant takes the seat on a plurality of 3,180 votes. Turnout below half is irrelevant to that rule, and nothing suggests the ward is shared.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify what proportional allocation guarantees about the origin of seats.
questions.stem: Under the proportional method used in your survey region, a party wins 8 per cent of the vote and receives four seats in a chamber of 50. What does the system guarantee about those seats?

options.text: That the four seats are concentrated in the districts where the party is strongest.
options.misconception: assumes proportional seats follow district strength

options.text: That each of the four seats is held by a member elected in the party's strongest ward.
options.misconception: confuses list allocation with local election

options.text: That the four seats arise from the party's share of the national vote, not from any single district.
That the party would receive the same four seats under any alternative allocation method.
options.misconception: assumes a proportional result is method-independent

questions.explanation: Under national list allocation the seats follow the party's overall vote share, and no district is responsible. The entitlement can differ under another method, so no guarantee extends to results under other rules.
questions.hint: Ask where the votes are counted.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a confidence-and-supply arrangement operates and ends.
questions.stem: In the assembly you are surveying, a minority government survives on the conditional votes of a second party. Explain how such an arrangement operates and how it can be brought to an end.

answer.exemplar: The arrangement is a standing exchange. The minority government needs votes for its budget and for any measure it wants to pass, and the second party supplies them in return for concessions on specified matters, most often a budget item, a review or a piece of legislation. Because the government depends on the partner for survival, the concessions are not voluntary gifts but the price of continuing, and they are usually negotiated in advance of the vote rather than after it. The arrangement ends in one of three ways. The partner may withdraw, either because a condition has been broken or because its own position has changed, and the government then either resigns or seeks an alternative. An election may produce a clearer mandate. Or a third party may supply enough votes to make the partner unnecessary, which dissolves the bargain without any formal ending to it. Throughout, the government remains in office and the partner remains outside it.

questions.explanation: The bargain exchanges needed votes for concessions, and holds only while the partner finds the price acceptable. It can end by withdrawal, by election, or when a third party makes the partner's support unnecessary.
questions.hint: Ask what the government gives to keep the votes.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the dividing line between new commitments and existing business.
questions.stem: During a caretaker period, a minister refuses to approve a new ten-year contract but signs a routine invoice for existing supplies. What does this behaviour show?

options.text: That the caretaker government is exercising powers reserved for a fully formed ministry.
options.misconception: assumes routine approvals are new policy decisions

options.text: That the caretaker government intends to seek a fresh mandate at the next election.
options.misconception: reads a refusal as an electoral strategy

options.text: That the caretaker government has been given a specific limit by the assembly.
options.misconception: infers a legal instruction from a prudential choice

options.text: That the caretaker distinction is between new commitments and the running of existing business.

questions.explanation: Refusing a new long contract while honouring an existing invoice shows the line between new commitments and current administration. A prudent minister may refuse on judgement, so the behaviour does not by itself prove a legal restriction.
questions.hint: Ask what distinguishes the two documents.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Design reforms that would open a cartel-dominated local party system.
questions.stem: Your survey region has two associations that have between them controlled every council seat for thirty years, while a third party that contested once in 1988 has long since dissolved. Propose reforms that would make a new party viable, and justify them.

answer.exemplar: Identify what the incumbent pair actually controls before designing anything. In this region the levers are the nomination lists, the chairing of committees and control of the hall where meetings are held. First, open the nomination process: any member in good standing should be able to be placed on a list without the consent of the existing officers, and a fixed proportion of places should be reserved for candidates who have not held an executive post. Second, break the chairing monopoly by allocating committee chairs in rotation rather than by custom, so a new member is not always seated behind the same two people. Third, make facilities accessible: any registered association should be able to book the hall on the same terms as the incumbents, and the booking register should be published. Fourth, support the difficult early years with a small, published campaign fund for parties contesting their first election. None of these measures guarantees a healthy opposition, but together they remove the specific points at which the incumbent pair's advantage becomes permanent.

questions.explanation: Reform should target the levers the incumbents hold: nomination, chairing and access to facilities. Opening each removes a point where advantage becomes permanent, though no single measure creates a viable opposition.
questions.hint: Find what the incumbents actually control.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish convergence of programmes from similarity of vote shares.
questions.stem: In the survey area the two main parties have noticeably similar positions, yet their vote shares differ by eleven points. What does that combination tell you?

options.text: Convergence concerns the content of programmes, not the size of each party's vote.
The parties are not really converging, because eleven points of difference is a large gap.
options.misconception: measures convergence by vote share rather than policy

options.text: The vote gap must be a counting error, since similar programmes usually produce similar votes.
options.misconception: assumes identical policies force identical vote shares

options.text: The smaller party has copied the larger one, since copying is the only way to explain both facts.
options.misconception: presumes imitation as the only route to similarity

questions.explanation: Convergence is a claim about the content of programmes, that the parties have moved close together on the issues that matter to the median voter. Vote shares can differ substantially even when programmes are close, because organisation, money and identity still count.
questions.hint: Ask what convergence is a claim about.

The secretary's report observes that the two winners both had contested a council seat before, and that the electorate had not previously included any member elected in the past two years.'

questions.stem: Which conclusion about the closed primary mechanism is best supported by the note?

options.misconception: assumes a closed primary favours public recognition

options.text: The mechanism tends to return candidates drawn from the established, already active membership.
The mechanism has widened the electorate, because the roll now includes newer members.
options.misconception: reads a membership roll as a widening of the electorate

options.text: The mechanism guarantees the winner will raise more money than the other candidates.
options.misconception: assumes a link between selection and fundraising

questions.explanation: Every candidate was a long-standing member and the roll excluded recent entrants, so the electorate was established activists. Both winners had contested a seat before, which is what a closed primary is expected to favour.
questions.hint: Look at who stood and who voted.

questions.learningObjective: State the accountability guarantee of a single-member district.
questions.stem: The survey region elects one member per district, and a candidate wins the district with 44 per cent of the vote. What does the single-member arrangement secure?

options.text: That the member will hold the seat until the next election, whatever happens in between.
options.misconception: confuses the guarantee with a complete term of office

options.text: That every party in the district will obtain some representation of its voters.
options.misconception: assumes a single-member seat delivers proportional shares

options.text: That the district is represented by one person with a personal mandate to represent it.
That the district's representative will have campaigned in every part of it during the election.
options.misconception: adds a campaign condition to the electoral arrangement

questions.explanation: A single-member district produces one representative with a personal mandate over the whole district, which is a guarantee about accountability rather than about the margin. It neither guarantees a term free of interruption nor any proportionality within the district.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the core property of a proportional allocation from a worked example.
questions.stem: A proportional system converts votes into seats, and a party that doubles its vote share from 15 to 30 per cent ends with more than twice as many seats. What does this demonstrate?

options.text: That proportional systems remove the distortions produced by constituency boundaries.
options.misconception: assumes proportionality erases all geographic bias

options.text: That proportional systems always reward the party with the largest national vote share.
options.misconception: conflates proportionality with a largest-party bonus

options.text: That the number of seats in the chamber is fixed by the size of the electorate.
options.misconception: infers chamber size from a change in vote share

options.text: That proportionality makes seat shares respond to changes in vote share.

questions.explanation: The example shows the defining property: seat shares move with vote shares, so doubling votes more than doubles seats. It says nothing about geographic bias or the size of the chamber.
questions.hint: Watch how the seat share responds.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a support-for-concessions pattern in a legislative record.

stimulus.body: Assembly record: 'The premier's bill to increase the licensing fee was opposed by the largest opposition party, which declared that it would vote with the government on the estimate but against the fee bill. Following the debate the estimate was agreed to and the fee bill was defeated. The premier thanked the largest opposition party for its support on the estimate and confirmed that the government would continue to seek its agreement on further financial business.'

questions.stem: What does the record show about the relationship between the government and the largest opposition party?

options.text: An arrangement in which support is given for some measures and withheld for others.
A coalition, because the two parties act together on the financial business of the assembly.
options.misconception: treats selective voting as a shared executive

options.text: A permanent agreement, because the premier has undertaken to seek the party's agreement henceforth.
options.misconception: reads an undertaking to consult as a fixed pact

options.text: Opposition to the government, because the opposition party defeated one of its bills.
options.misconception: assumes defeating one bill ends all cooperation

questions.explanation: The record shows support on the estimate and opposition on the fee bill, which is the essence of confidence and supply: support is given selectively in return for continued government. That is neither a coalition nor a permanent pact.
questions.hint: Look at how support is used across measures.

questions.learningObjective: Judge observed administrative conduct against the caretaker standard.

stimulus.body: Observation at the county offices: 'A notice has been posted announcing the closure of the outdated footbridge repair scheme, and a tender is being prepared for the archive roof. The outgoing chief executive has said that no new contracts will be signed beyond the routine renewal of existing ones, and that the incoming administration will be told which projects have already been announced.'

questions.stem: Which reading of the observations best fits?

options.text: The administration is acting as a caretaker, because it has stopped all new project work entirely.
options.misconception: reads a limit on new commitments as a total freeze

options.text: The administration is acting as a caretaker, keeping current work going but avoiding fresh commitments.
The administration is preparing a programme for the next election, since the tender work is campaign-directed.
options.misconception: assumes electoral purpose from routine administrative activity

options.text: The administration is fully in power, since a caretaker could not announce any closure or tender.
options.misconception: denies a caretaker any administrative capacity

questions.explanation: Announcing closures and preparing tenders for existing work is the conduct of current business, and the stated refusal to sign new contracts beyond routine renewals is the caretaker limit. It is not a total freeze of activity, nor does it imply a caretaker cannot act.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the order of filling offices affects a party's character.
questions.stem: Explain, for a briefing note, why the order in which a party fills its leadership offices can affect the character of the party that results.

answer.exemplar: The order decides which office is filled on the basis of which. Where a leader is elected first and then appoints colleagues, the leader's judgement shapes the team, and the party tends to be cohesive around one person's priorities at the cost of the range a wider selection might have produced. Where the committee or membership is elected first and the leader is chosen by that body, the choice is constrained by a wider brief, and the party is more likely to reflect a negotiated programme. Where the leader is appointed from outside the membership, the party gains fresh perspective but loses the base of internal commitment that usually supplies campaign energy. The order also affects accountability. An elected leader can be challenged by the members who chose them, while an appointee can be replaced at the next review without any need to persuade the membership.

questions.explanation: The order determines what is filled on the basis of what, so a leader-first sequence concentrates choice in one person. It also shapes accountability, since an elected leader can be challenged by those who chose them.
questions.hint: Ask which choice constrains the other.

options.misconception: assumes a rotation implies rivalry

options.text: A democratic meritocracy, because every applicant is refused on identical grounds.
options.misconception: equates identical refusal with meritocratic selection

A temporary shortage of candidates, which will clear itself within a generation.
options.misconception: assumes an absence of applicants is accidental

questions.explanation: A small group that shares office across generations while no outsider has ever applied is a closed elite, and the absence of applicants is a product of the arrangement rather than a shortage of interest. Rotation among the few does not make the selection open.

options.misconception: treats one difference as the absence of convergence

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Design a leadership selection open to new members without losing order.
questions.stem: Your county party wants a leadership selection that new members can win but that does not turn the contest into an open popularity poll. Propose a rule set, and justify how it meets both aims.

answer.exemplar: Separate the eligibility to stand from the size of the electorate, because these are the two levers that a closed primary usually pulls together. Allow any member in good standing to be nominated, with a modest signature requirement and a published timetable, so that a new member is not screened out before voters see a name. Then set the electorate by a rule that values both continuity and fresh participation: for example, a ballot in which each member has one vote, with a weighting that increases for members who have organised branch activity in the past two years, and with a minimum share of the voting weight reserved for members joined within that period. Publish the count immediately, and require the winner to be confirmed by a meeting of branches rather than by a single executive vote, so the result cannot be overturned in private. The result should be a selection that is open in access, deliberate in weighting and transparent in the count.

questions.explanation: A closed primary usually restricts standing and voting together, so separating them opens access without an open poll. A weighted ballot and a published count keep some weight with continuity and prevent private overturn.
questions.hint: Treat standing and voting as separate levers.

Three members, one from each polling ward, because each ward counts separately.

questions.hint: Ask how many seats the district returns.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits of what proportional allocation can guarantee.
questions.stem: Your briefing note must set out for the district council what a proportional system can and cannot achieve, using the seat totals in the last election as the example.

answer.exemplar: The seat totals show the achievement clearly. A party that won 31 per cent of the vote holds 30 of the 100 seats, and the second party with 27 per cent holds 27, so within a seat or two the chamber reflects the votes. What the system cannot do is represent every area in the way a single-member constituency would. Because the list is drawn across the whole region, a party may be strong in a district and still place no candidate who lives there, and the member who does sit for that district will have been chosen by votes from the whole region rather than from it. Nor does the system guarantee that any particular party can win at all, because a threshold may exclude small parties from the list altogether. Proportionality is about the aggregate, and it is silent about the local.

questions.explanation: The seat totals show seats tracking votes closely, which is the system's achievement. It cannot guarantee local representation, because lists are drawn across the whole region rather than from each district.
questions.hint: Ask whether the claim is about totals or places.

questions.hint: Follow which actor acts at each stage.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the paired controls that make a party system closed.
questions.stem: An association you survey accepts no new members without the approval of two long-standing members, and its officers are elected only by those who joined before a stated year. Which features does this combine?

options.text: Restricted entry to the membership and restricted choice of the officers.
An open membership with a carefully designed election for the officers.
options.misconception: treats admission controls as a feature of the election

options.text: A democratic organisation in which every member votes on every decision.
options.misconception: confuses a limited electorate with direct democracy

options.text: A movement in which the officers are chosen to represent competing local groups.
options.misconception: assumes division into groups implies an open contest

questions.explanation: The two controls work together: admission needs approval and the officers are chosen by the earlier generation. A cartel in this sense restricts both who is inside and who chooses the leadership.
questions.hint: Ask who may join and who may choose.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the conditions under which two-party competition produces convergence.
questions.stem: In the district you survey, the two main parties have converged on the two most visible issues but remain far apart on two duller ones. Explain the conditions that produce this pattern and what would change it.

answer.exemplar: Convergence of this kind occurs when the two parties compete for the same decisive group of voters and the issues that decide those elections are few, salient and well understood. In the district the road levy and the hospital closure command attention, so both parties have calculated that the median voter will punish a position far from theirs on either, and the proposals move towards each other. On the drainage catchment rules and the notice period for allotment rent, attention is thinner and the cost of disagreement is borne by fewer voters, so the parties can hold different positions without paying for it. Two things would change the pattern. A significant number of voters shifting their priorities would move the decisive issue and pull the convergence elsewhere with it, and a party that won a national or regional share of attention on one of the dull issues could separate itself without paying the electoral price.

questions.explanation: Convergence concentrates on the salient issues that decide the election for the decisive group of voters. The parties can differ where attention is thin, and a shift in voter priorities would move the convergence.
questions.hint: Ask which issues command attention.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Read a selection rule set and identify the electorate it defines.

stimulus.body: Extract from the branch rules: 'A candidate for the branch's selection to the county council must be proposed by not fewer than ten members of the branch in good standing and must have been a member for at least two years. The ballot is conducted among members in good standing at the date of the closing of nominations. The branch rules further provide that any member may be present at the count and may request the inclusion of an additional candidate before the ballot is despatched.'

questions.stem: What does the extract show about the branch's selection mechanism?

options.text: An open selection, because any member may request that another candidate be included.
options.misconception: reads a right to nominate as a right to vote

options.text: A closed selection, since voting is confined to members at the closing of nominations.
A delegate-based election, because the ballot is despatched to members rather than cast in person.
options.misconception: confuses a postal ballot with a delegate election

options.text: An open nomination with a closed vote, since the two stages use different rules.
options.misconception: treats differing rules as evidence of an open election

questions.explanation: Voting is confined to members in good standing at the closing of nominations, which is a closed electorate, and the candidate requirements tighten it further. The right to request an additional candidate affects who may stand rather than who may vote.
questions.hint: Check who casts the ballot.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the cost of a single-member guarantee in a scattered district.
questions.stem: Your survey district returns one member, and a decision is needed on whether to create a second seat for its scattered settlements. What does the single-member arrangement tell you about the trade-off?

options.text: That adding a second seat would automatically double the area any one member can cover.
options.misconception: assumes more seats means smaller districts by itself

options.text: That one member must be chosen from each settlement, since the district is geographically scattered.
options.misconception: invents a settlement rule the arrangement does not contain

options.text: That one member carries the whole area, so accessibility for the scattered part is the cost of the arrangement.
That the scattered settlements already have separate representation elsewhere in the legislature.
options.misconception: assumes coverage that the scenario never states

questions.explanation: A single member represents the whole district, and that personal responsibility is what the arrangement provides. Its cost is that the scattered settlements are answerable to one person, which is exactly the problem a second seat would address.
questions.hint: Ask who represents the scattered areas.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State what a threshold and a divisor method do to a proportional allocation.

stimulus.body: Note on the last allocation: 'The chamber has 60 seats. The party with 42 per cent of the vote received 25 seats, the party with 26 per cent received 16, and a party with 4 per cent received no seat, as the method applies a threshold of 5 per cent. The method is a highest averages divisor, so seats are assigned at the level of the whole list, and no candidate is elected from a single district in the way a first-past-the-post seat would be.'

questions.stem: Which statement does the note support?

options.text: Every party with some support is guaranteed a place in the chamber.
options.misconception: ignores the threshold the note states

options.text: The chamber's composition is identical to what a first-past-the-post allocation would produce.
options.misconception: equates a list method with a constituency method

options.text: The party with 42 per cent of the vote has a majority of seats in the chamber.
options.misconception: confuses a large plurality of votes with a seat majority

options.text: Seats follow the vote shares at the level of the list, subject to a threshold for small parties.

questions.explanation: The note shows a divisor method working on the whole list, so seats track vote shares, with a threshold. Neither the 42 per cent nor the 25 seats is a majority, and the two methods are not equivalent.
questions.hint: Note the method and the threshold.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a conditional term attached to a supply agreement.
questions.stem: A minority government is told by its partner that a supply agreement ends if the government loses a confidence vote. What does this condition tell you about the arrangement?

options.text: The agreement is conditional, so the government's survival rests on the partner's continued support.
The agreement is void, because no party may be threatened with the loss of an office.
options.misconception: assumes a constitutional prohibition on political pressure

options.text: The partner has become a member of the government, since it now holds a veto over its survival.
options.misconception: confuses a condition of support with an executive seat

options.text: The government must hold a fresh election, because only voters may end a supply agreement.
options.misconception: assumes only electors can terminate a political bargain

questions.explanation: A condition attached to the supply makes the arrangement conditional rather than permanent. The government is thereby dependent on the partner's continuing goodwill, though the partner gains no executive seat.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the agreement on a defeat.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the circumstances and limits that produce a caretaker government.
questions.stem: Explain, for a briefing note, under what circumstances a caretaker government arises, what it is permitted to do, and why those permissions are drawn as they are.

answer.exemplar: A caretaker government arises when an election has been held and no party can command a workable majority, and the time required to negotiate a new government or to resolve the count is thought to require continuity in office. Its remit is set by convention and, in some systems, by law, and it is drawn around the distinction between administering what exists and deciding what should exist. Existing contracts are honoured, current law is administered, elections are run, and the assembly is summoned. New programmes, major spending decisions and long-term undertakings are excluded. The reason for the line is that a caretaker has no mandate to commit the state, and every decision it takes that binds a successor is a decision taken without a mandate and one that will be judged against the standards of the incoming government. Where the emergency is real, as in a collapse of government during a crisis, the convention widens and each act is required to be justified and recorded.

questions.explanation: A caretaker arises when no party can command a majority after an election and continuity is needed. Its remit covers administering what exists rather than deciding what should exist, because it cannot bind a successor.
questions.hint: Ask what a government without a mandate may do.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify an order of selection within a single meeting.
questions.stem: A party fills its two main offices in a single meeting, but the treasurer must be selected before the leader can be installed in the chair. Which order applies?

options.text: The leader is chosen first, and the treasurer is then appointed by the new leader.
options.misconception: reverses the sequence the scenario states

options.text: The treasurer is chosen first, and the leader is installed afterwards in the chair.
Both offices are decided simultaneously, because a single meeting settles all questions.
options.misconception: ignores the stated sequence within one meeting

options.text: The chair is filled by the previous holder, since the treasurer's role is merely ceremonial.
options.misconception: assumes a ceremonial office from no evidence given

questions.explanation: Because the treasurer is selected before the leader is installed, the order is treasurer first, leader second. A single meeting does not make the sequence simultaneous.
questions.hint: Ask which decision must come first.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify control of nominations as a cartel feature.
questions.stem: The survey region's dominant association has never opposed a council decision in twenty years, and its officers are the only candidates nominated in six of seven wards. Which feature is being displayed?

options.text: A disciplined opposition, because the association votes together on every matter.
options.misconception: confuses internal discipline with opposition to others

options.text: A single-issue focus, because the association campaigns on one policy only.
options.misconception: infers a narrow programme from a voting pattern

options.text: Control of who can stand for office, which keeps competitors out of most contests.
A democratic nomination process, since six of seven wards use the same rule.
options.misconception: mistakes consistency for openness

questions.explanation: The decisive feature is control of the candidate lists in six of seven wards, leaving no competitor in those contests. A party that votes its own way is not thereby opposing others, and a consistent rule is not an open one.
questions.hint: Ask who is able to stand.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Support an explanation of convergence from an editorial's reasoning.

stimulus.body: Excerpt from a local newspaper's editorial: 'The two parties have once again moved to the same position on the harbour dredging, and once again differ on the parish boundary. The dredging question decides elections here, so neither can risk a stand that costs it the harbour vote. The boundary question, which has produced two legal challenges and almost no comment, is one they can afford to disagree about, since the votes it affects are concentrated in a single ward that both parties already hold.'

questions.stem: The editorial supports which explanation of the parties' positions?

options.text: The parties have simply copied one another, since no one has explained the agreement.
options.misconception: explains similarity by imitation rather than incentive

options.text: The parties disagree where they can, because the harbour question is settled by law.
options.misconception: invents a legal settlement the extract never mentions

options.text: The parties converge where votes are spread across wards and differ where they are concentrated.
options.misconception: reverses which pattern follows from voter concentration

options.text: The parties converge where the median voter is engaged, and the boundary vote sits in one ward.

questions.explanation: Agreement is attributed to the dredging question deciding elections, and disagreement to one affecting few votes. Convergence follows the intensity of the median voter's interest, not the number of wards involved.
questions.hint: Ask where the decisive vote lies.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess a proposal to replace a single-member district with a multi-member list.
questions.stem: A proposal would abolish the single-member arrangement in your survey region and replace it with a multi-member district allocating three seats by proportional list. Evaluate the proposal for a briefing note.

answer.exemplar: The proposal trades a personal guarantee for an aggregate one, and the trade should be judged on that basis. The single-member district guarantees that one person is answerable for the whole area, which is what allows a constituent in a scattered hamlet to point to a named representative with a duty of care towards them. A three-seat list replaces that with a guarantee that the composition of the delegation reflects the district's vote shares, which protects smaller local interests against a dominant party but produces members with no particular constituency and no individual duty to anyone. The strongest version of the proposal's case is that the current arrangement has produced long neglect of the outer settlements, since a member with a secure seat in the main town has little incentive to travel. The strongest objection is that the alternative fixes neglect by dissolving responsibility, and that the better response is to redraw the single-member districts so that the scattered settlements form a seat of their own.

questions.explanation: The proposal exchanges a personal duty of care for proportional composition, and treats neglect by dissolving responsibility. Redrawing single-member districts would reach the same end without removing the personal guarantee.
questions.hint: Compare the two guarantees being exchanged.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Qualify the guarantee offered by a proportional allocation system.
questions.stem: Under a proportional method, a party with 5 per cent of the vote receives no seats, and a party with 6 per cent receives two. What does this reveal about the guarantee proportionality offers?

options.text: It is a relationship between totals, and it can be qualified by rules that exclude small parties.
It is a relationship between individual districts, and it excludes parties that lose them.
options.misconception: confuses the aggregate guarantee with a local one

options.text: It is a promise of representation for any party that wins a single district.
options.misconception: assumes district representation follows from proportional lists

options.text: It is a guarantee that every vote cast is converted into a proportionate share of seats.
options.misconception: overstates the guarantee by ignoring the threshold

questions.explanation: The example shows proportionality as a relationship between overall totals, with a threshold excluding small parties. It does not guarantee every vote is converted, and it says nothing about any single district.
questions.hint: Ask what the guarantee covers and what it excludes.
